analysis.one_liner: Redirects federal foster care money toward keeping children safely at home with family instead of institutions.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 4, 2017 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, the bill never received a markup or a vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let states spend federal foster care dollars on mental health care, substance abuse treatment, and in-home parenting programs for children at risk of being removed from their homes, rather than paying only after a child is taken into state care. It would cut off federal payments for group and institutional placements after two weeks unless the placement passes an independent assessment, pushing the child welfare system toward family homes and kin caregivers. It also funds kinship navigator programs, eases interstate placements for foster children, and reauthorizes existing child welfare programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Children at risk of entering foster care and their parents, especially families affected by the opioid epidemic; grandparents and other relatives caring for children; pregnant and parenting foster youth; and foster children needing placement across state lines, all of whom get services and placements aimed at keeping or reuniting families instead of institutional beds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: At-risk children, parents, and kin caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Lets states use federal Title IV-E foster care funds for mental health and substance abuse prevention and treatment and in-home parenting programs for children who can stay safely at home, instead of funding only out-of-home placements [S2][S3].

Allows federal foster care maintenance payments while a child stays with a parent in a licensed family-based residential substance abuse treatment facility, for up to 12 months, keeping families together during treatment [S3].
Provides a 50 percent federal match for evidence-based kinship navigator programs that help relatives caring for children find services [S2][S3].

Cuts off federal support for group and institutional placements after two weeks unless the child is in a qualified residential treatment program with a 30-day independent assessment and judicial approval, pushing placements toward family settings [S3].

Eliminates the 15-month limit on family reunification services while a child is in foster care and funds an electronic interstate case-processing system to speed up placements of children across state lines [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Residential group-care providers lose a guaranteed federal revenue stream for housing children in institutions; states must keep prevention spending at 2014 levels and pay for new assessments; adoptive families face a delayed scheduled increase in adoption assistance payments used to offset the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Group homes, states, and some adoptive families

drawbacks.text: The bill delays the scheduled phase-in of higher federal adoption assistance payments (a cost-of-living increase approved in 2008) to help pay for the new prevention services, reducing what some adoptive families receive [S3].

Restricting federal payments for congregate placements could leave children with serious emotional or behavioral disorders without enough appropriate beds; the bill itself requires states to certify they will not push youth into the juvenile justice system as a result and orders a GAO study of that risk [S3].
States that elect the prevention option must hold their own prevention spending at 2014 levels and may not count it toward the federal match, which limits states facing budget pressure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the bill moves federal money from paying for institutional care after removal toward services that keep families together, which child welfare research generally favors. The real trade-offs are the delayed adoption assistance increase, the risk that congregate-care restrictions outpace the supply of foster homes for children with acute needs, and new administrative burdens on states.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and its Human Resources subcommittee for two years without a markup, a vote, or a report, and died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 4, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
On January 13, 2017 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Human Resources, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no report before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For the remainder of the 115th Congress, providers of congregate and institutional foster care kept the existing open-ended federal funding stream for housing children in group settings, which this bill would have curtailed; families awaiting prevention services got nothing from this bill's inaction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and ranking Democratic Ways and Means member Sander Levin as its two introducers, and its 8 cosponsors split 7 Democrats to 1 Republican; no opposition appears anywhere in the record [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Congregate and residential foster care providers (group homes, child-care institutions)
industries.note: The bill cuts off federal foster care payments for group and institutional placements after two weeks unless the child is in an accredited, assessed qualified residential treatment program, directly reducing revenue that comes from housing children in institutions rather than family homes [S3]. Under the status quo that prevailed when the bill died, these providers kept the funding stream unchanged.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance abuse treatment providers
industries.note: The bill opens a 50 percent federal match for clinicians delivering trauma-informed mental health and substance abuse services and in-home parenting programs to children at risk of removal and their parents — a large new funding stream for behavioral health care [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Kinship navigator programs and private child welfare agencies
industries.note: Evidence-based kinship navigator programs become federally reimbursable at 50 percent, and for-profit and nonprofit child welfare providers are named as eligible partners in regional grants for families affected by substance abuse [S3].

industries.industry: Independent accrediting bodies (CARF, Joint Commission, COA)
industries.note: Qualified residential treatment programs must hold accreditation from one of these approved organizations to keep receiving federal payments, making accreditation a federal funding gate [S3].
